newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania leader hails Moldova election outcome.
newsitem.headline: Romania leader hails Moldova election outcome.

text.p: Romania's new president Emil Constantinescu on Tuesday said the outcome of elections in Moldova could cement relations between Bucharest and the territory it lost during World War Two.

But nationalists and many newspapers were less optimistic. Some said the weekend victory in presidential polls by Petru Lucinschi, who says his close ties with Moscow will help the former Soviet republic, was a throwback to communist rule which would bury forever any hope of reunification.
Constantinescu, who won a presidential election himself last month by ousting ex-communists, told Lucinschi the two men could develop "special privileged relations".
The ultimate aim, he said in a telegram from the European security summit in Portugal, was "to draw our countries closer and ensure their success in building democracy and reform".
Moldova is made up mostly of the territory of Bessarabia taken from Romania by the Kremlin under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact. Nearly two-thirds of its residents are ethnic Romanians.
But Post-Communist authorities in Romania appear less concerned with ethnic kin in Moldova than with their main foreign policy objective of NATO and European Union membership.

A former top communist and chairman of parliament, Lucinschi was viewed as more favourable to Moscow than defeated incumbent Mircea Snegur. He told Moldovans after his win that he would "use my ties in Moscow for the good of the country".
Romania has yet to sign friendship treaties with ex-Soviet republics to the east -- Moldova, Ukraine and Russia -- which reject its demand for a public apology over the 1939 pact.

Talk of recreating the "Greater Romania" of the early 20th century was widespread after the end of Soviet rule. It has largely died down in both Romania and Moldova, though Bucharest politicians are concerned about Russian influence in the area.
The leader of the Greater Romania Party, which won five percent of the vote in last month's Romanian general election, said it was too early to judge Lucinschi's motives.
"Snegur deserved to lose because he did nothing to promote the unionist cause," Corneliu Vadim Tudor said by telephone.
"If Lucinschi has a secret plan to win Moscow's approval to join Moldova and Romania, he might be the man of providence. If his plan is to pull it back to Russia, history will curse him."
Many Bucharest dailies were less charitable.
"A step backwards in Chisinau," screamed the headline in the liberal newspaper Romania Libera. "Pro-Russian candidate tricks Bessarabian voters," echoed the popular daily Ziua.
The independent Adevarul, more cautious, said Lucinschi had differed with leftists "who never hid anti-Romanian sentiments and started the most odious 'Romanophobic' campaign ever seen".
But Constantinescu's main priority to the east appeared to be resuming talks with Ukraine to conclude the stalled treaty.
"Romanians must know that the treaty with Ukraine is one of the criteria for NATO membership," he told Romanian television in Lisbon after talks with Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma.
